passage: Kishore stood at his uncle's shop counter in the kasba, tongue pressed hard against his cheek, counting coins for a customer's change. Gurleen, waiting with an empty bag for lentils, watched the little bulge. “Are you making fun of me?” she asked. “No, I'm counting,” he said, without looking up. When he finished he handed her the bag and said, with a very serious face, “Our lentils are so good the goats queue up to buy them.” His cheek bulged again and his eyes crinkled. Gurleen laughed. “That's a joke!”

qa.q: What did Kishore press against his cheek while counting coins?
qa.a: He pressed his tongue against his cheek.

qa.q: What might Kishore's cheek bulge mean the second time, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Probably that he was holding back a joke, since his face was very serious while his eyes crinkled. The first time it was concentration, and it could also simply be a habit.

qa.q: How could Gurleen tell which meaning it was?
qa.a: By looking at the context: the first time he was counting and looked down, the second time he spoke solemnly with crinkled eyes, and she could ask if unsure.

qa.q: How did Gurleen see the first bulge?
qa.a: She wondered if he was making fun of her, so the same cue looked mocking to her at first. 🙂

grounding: A tongue pressed in the cheek can mean concentration or a hidden joke, depending on context.

passage: In the art room, Yuki pressed her tongue into her cheek as she drew a careful curve for the fish's tail. Ms Olga walked between the tables. The class had been loud all morning, chairs scraping and voices rising. She pushed her own tongue into her cheek and said, “Well, this is the quietest class we've had all year.” The children who knew her giggled. Yuki grinned. A new boy near the door looked up and put a finger to his lips, worried he was being told off.

qa.q: What did Yuki press into her cheek while drawing?
qa.a: She pressed her tongue into her cheek.

qa.q: What did Ms Olga's tongue in her cheek suggest she meant, and how might a newcomer read it?
qa.a: That she meant the opposite, since the room was loud, and the children who knew her giggled. A newcomer without that shared context might take it literally.

qa.q: How could Ms Olga make her joke clearer to a newcomer?
qa.a: She could add a smile or a word, or quietly explain later that she was joking.

qa.q: How might the new boy feel when he puts a finger to his lips?
qa.a: Worried and confused, thinking he was being told off, because he did not know her style or the shared joke.

grounding: A tongue in the cheek can mean concentration or a joke, and the meaning depends on shared context.

subtype: Blank face at bullying or shame [Regulating]
passage:
“How was school?” asked Dhruv, dropping his bag.
“Fine,” said Yogesh, his face flat as a wall.
“Your face is doing the wall thing. Did somebody say something?”
Yogesh looked at the floor. “They call me Stick. I just look at nothing so they get bored.”
“Does it work?”
“A bit. It also feels like a stone in my stomach.”
“I'm glad you told me. Want me to come and talk to Sir?”
“Maybe. Not yet.”
“Okay. I'll ask again tomorrow.”

qa.q: What do the boys call Yogesh?
qa.a: They call him Stick.

qa.q: What is Yogesh feeling behind his blank face?
qa.a: Hurt, and probably ashamed, since he says it feels like a stone in his stomach. He keeps his face still so the boys get bored and stop.

qa.q: What could Dhruv do next?
qa.a: Respect Yogesh's pace, keep checking in, and be ready to go with him to talk to Sir when he is ready.

qa.q: How might Dhruv see his brother's blank face?
qa.a: He can tell it is not calm, since he calls it “the wall thing”, so he is probably worried and wants to help.

grounding: A child keeps a blank face when teased; an adult checks in privately and offers help.

subtype: Blank face at bullying or shame [Regulating]
passage: I'm Dilnaz. When the girls at the bus stop laughed about my haircut, I made my face like a stone. I didn't blink or smile. Inside I was shaking. At lunch I didn't eat, and Maria Ma'am, my class teacher, noticed. She sat down beside me and said quietly, “The bus stop seemed hard today. You can tell me, or you can help me with the library books. Either is fine.” I chose the books. After a while I said, “They laughed at my hair.” She said, “Thank you for telling me. You can come to me any time.”

qa.q: What did Maria Ma'am ask Dilnaz to help with as an alternative to talking?
qa.a: She offered that Dilnaz could help her with the library books.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling behind her stone face?
qa.a: Hurt and ashamed, since she says inside she was shaking. She kept her face blank so as not to give the girls a reaction.

qa.q: What did Maria Ma'am do that made it easier to talk?
qa.a: She spoke quietly and privately, gave Dilnaz a choice and an easy task, and said she could come any time.

qa.q: How might the girls at the bus stop have read Dilnaz's stone face?
qa.a: They may have thought she did not care, and not seen the hurt behind it.

grounding: A child holds a blank face when teased, which hides real hurt; a private check-in helps.

passage: The school canteen was so loud that everyone shouted. New boy Eshaan sat down next to Chinmay, who said, with a perfectly straight face, “I trained my pet elephant to do my homework, but he ate the notebook.” Chinmay's old friends laughed. Eshaan leaned in. “Really?” Chinmay held the flat face a second longer, then one eyebrow twitched. “No. I don't have an elephant.” Eshaan laughed with relief. Chinmay said, “Sorry. I should smile when I do that, so people know.” He tried a tiny smile, and it looked funny too.

qa.q: What did Chinmay say the elephant ate?
qa.a: He said the elephant ate the notebook.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling when he said “Really?”, and what else could it have been?
qa.a: Confused and unsure, since the noisy canteen and Chinmay's flat face gave no clear sign it was a joke. He might also have been trying to be polite to someone he had just met.

qa.q: What small signal could help Chinmay make his jokes clearer?
qa.a: A twinkle in the eyes or a tiny smile, as he says he should do, so newcomers can tell it is a joke.

qa.q: How might Chinmay's old friends see the same joke?
qa.a: They know his style, so the flat face is part of what makes it funny for them.

grounding: A deadpan joke is funnier to those who know the style and confusing to others; a small signal helps.

passage:
“Nilesh, your homework?” said Mr Menon, holding out his hand.
“The dog ate it,” said Nilesh, without any expression. “He said it was hard to digest.”
Mr Menon's eyebrows rose. Several children giggled and Gurleen snorted. Nilesh took the notebook from his bag, the corner of his mouth twitching. “Here.”
Mr Menon studied him. “You have a very good straight face. Next time give me a smile as well, so I know.”
“Yes, sir,” said Nilesh. His eyes were bright.

qa.q: Who snorted when Nilesh said the dog ate his homework?
qa.a: Gurleen snorted.

qa.q: What was Mr Menon probably feeling when Nilesh said the dog ate it, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Probably puzzled or doubtful for a moment, since there was no sign it was a joke. His comment about a good straight face suggests he then saw the humour.

qa.q: What small signal could Nilesh add next time?
qa.a: A smile or a twinkle in his eyes, as Mr Menon asks, so people who do not know his style can tell it is a joke.

qa.q: How might Gurleen see Nilesh's joke differently from Mr Menon?
qa.a: She seems to know his style, so the flat face makes it funnier for her, while the teacher has to work out whether it is real.

grounding: A deadpan joke is funny to those who know the style and confusing to others.

subtype: Bowing the head and namaste in India [Mismatch]
passage:
At the village temple, Lavanya joined her palms and bowed her head to the priest's wife, as she'd been taught. The old lady smiled and put a hand near her head in blessing, and Lavanya looked up, smiling too. Sarika, her friend, saw it all.
Later, in class, the teacher scolded the whole row for the noise. Lavanya's head went down again, but her shoulders sagged and her eyes were wet. Sarika frowned. It was the same head, bent the same way, but it looked very different. She moved her chair closer.

qa.q: Whom did Lavanya greet with namaste at the temple?
qa.a: She greeted the priest's wife.

qa.q: What might Lavanya's bowed head in class mean compared with the temple, and how sure can Sarika be?
qa.a: At the temple it was respect; in class, with sagging shoulders and wet eyes, it looked like embarrassment or upset. Sarika cannot be certain and might need to ask.

qa.q: What could Sarika do next?
qa.a: Ask Lavanya quietly how she is, or just sit near her, since the bent head alone does not say what she feels.

qa.q: How might the priest's wife see Lavanya's bow?
qa.a: As respect and a warm greeting, since she smiled and offered a blessing.

grounding: Bowing the head with namaste shows respect, unlike a head bowed in shame; context tells them apart.

subtype: Bowing the head and namaste in India [Mismatch]
passage:
At the school assembly in Toronto, the visiting teacher Mr Rao joined his palms and gave the principal a small bow of the head. Paulo, in the second row, nudged his neighbour Soo-ah. “Is he in trouble?” he whispered. “Why?” “His head's down.”
Soo-ah shook her head. “No, it's a greeting. My neighbour does it. It's called namaste, and it means respect.”
Paulo looked again. Mr Rao was smiling, and the principal had joined her palms back. “Oh,” whispered Paulo. “I thought he was sad.”

qa.q: Who greeted the principal with namaste?
qa.a: Mr Rao, the visiting teacher, greeted the principal with namaste.

qa.q: What did Paulo think Mr Rao's bowed head meant, and what did he learn?
qa.a: He thought it meant Mr Rao was in trouble or sad, as a bowed head can show shame. He learned it was a respectful greeting when he saw Mr Rao smiling.

qa.q: What could Paulo do next time he is unsure what a gesture means?
qa.a: Look at the face and setting, or ask someone kindly, as he did with Soo-ah.

qa.q: How might Mr Rao see his own greeting?
qa.a: As an ordinary sign of respect he uses without thinking, since he was smiling. He may not realise it can look different to someone new. 🙂

grounding: A bowed head with namaste is respect in India, unlike a bowed head in shame; culture and context decide.

passage:
Monday: Anirban told Jeevan Sir why his homework was late, and Sir tilted his head. Anirban thought, He's listening and he's sorry for me, and he explained the whole story.
Wednesday: Anirban said he had finished all the sums. Sir tilted his head again and said nothing. Anirban's stomach clenched: Does he think I'm lying? “Show me your working for number seven,” said Sir, in an easy voice. Anirban showed him, and Sir nodded.
Friday: Anirban watched Sir tilt his head at a friend. Sir's eyes were warm. “Tell me more,” he said. Anirban smiled a little. The tilt was the same, but the tone told him more.

qa.q: What did Jeevan Sir ask Anirban to show him on Wednesday?
qa.a: He asked him to show his working for number seven.

qa.q: What did Anirban think Sir's head tilt meant on Monday and on Wednesday?
qa.a: On Monday he read it as listening and sympathy, so he explained everything. On Wednesday he read it as doubt and his stomach clenched, though Sir may just have been curious.

qa.q: What could Anirban do when he is not sure what a head tilt means?
qa.a: Notice the tone and face that come with it, and ask a question if he is unsure, like “Is something wrong with my answer?”

qa.q: How might Jeevan Sir see his own head tilt?
qa.a: Probably as a sign that he is listening and thinking, without realising it can look like doubt to a nervous child.

grounding: A head tilt can show curiosity, sympathy or doubt; tone and body add the meaning.

passage:
“When I was ten,” said Gautam Nana, “my teacher Mrs Pillai tilted her head when I said I had not copied Ramesh's sum. My heart sank. I thought, She doesn't believe me. I stood there stiff as a post.”
“What happened?” asked Jaya.
“She said, in a kind voice, ‘Tell me how you got it.’ I showed her my working and her face cleared. The tilt was only because she wanted to hear more.” He smiled. “Now when a teacher tilts her head I remember the tone. It can be curiosity, or sympathy, or doubt. You have to look at the whole face.”

qa.q: Who tilted her head when Gautam said he had not copied?
qa.a: Mrs Pillai tilted her head.

qa.q: What did young Gautam think the head tilt meant, and what did it turn out to be?
qa.a: He thought it meant Mrs Pillai did not believe him, since his heart sank. It turned out she wanted to hear more.

qa.q: What could Jaya learn from Nana's story?
qa.a: That a head tilt has several possible meanings, so she should look at the whole face and tone, and offer her working or explanation.

qa.q: How might Mrs Pillai have seen Gautam's stiff face?
qa.a: Probably as worry, and she did not intend doubt. Her kind “Tell me how you got it” suggests she wanted to put him at ease.

grounding: A head tilt in a teacher may be curiosity, sympathy or doubt; tone and the whole face add meaning.

passage: Tomas walked off the pitch with his shoulders dropped and his eyes on the grass. His team had lost the final, one goal to nothing. His coach, Mateo, jogged after him. “Cheer up, it's only a game!” Tomas shrugged and kept walking. Mateo slowed down, then sat next to him on the bench. “That save you made in the second half was a tough one. I know you worked so hard.” Tomas's shoulders eased a little and he leaned against the bench. “I wanted to win,” he said, quietly.

qa.q: What was the score in the final?
qa.a: His team lost the final, one goal to nothing.

qa.q: What was Tomas feeling as he walked off with his shoulders dropped, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Sadness and disappointment about the loss, since he kept his eyes on the grass. He may also have been tired after the match.

qa.q: What worked better from Mateo, telling him to cheer up or sitting beside him?
qa.a: Sitting beside him and naming his effort worked better, because Tomas's shoulders eased and he said he wanted to win. “Cheer up” made him shrug and walk on.

qa.q: How might Mateo have felt about the loss?
qa.a: Probably disappointed too, and worried about Tomas. His first “Cheer up” may have been an awkward try to help.

grounding: A child drops the shoulders after a loss; a warm word helps more than telling him to cheer up.

passage: In the hostel common room, Sunaina held her maths paper face down on her knees, her shoulders rounded like a shell. Nandini, on the next chair, saw the number on the top corner before Sunaina covered it. It was lower than either of them had expected. “Cheer up,” said another girl, passing by. Sunaina pulled her knees up. Nandini said nothing for a minute, then moved her chair closer. “That was a hard paper. I got stuck on the last question too.” Sunaina let out a breath. “I studied so much.”

qa.q: Where was Sunaina sitting with her maths paper?
qa.a: She was in the hostel common room.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling with her shoulders rounded and the paper face down, and what else might it be?
qa.a: Sadness and disappointment about the mark, and maybe embarrassment, since she covered it and pulled her knees up. She may also have been tired from studying.

qa.q: What did Nandini do that helped, unlike the girl who said “Cheer up”?
qa.a: She stayed quietly close and shared that she too got stuck, which let Sunaina say how she felt. The other girl's words brushed the feeling aside.

qa.q: How might Nandini be feeling herself?
qa.a: She may be a bit disappointed and worried for her friend too, since she got stuck on the last question as well.

grounding: A child drops the shoulders after disappointing marks; a warm word helps more than cheer up.

passage: Thomas's diary, Thursday. Asked Chinmay today if he wanted to join my cricket team. He lifted one shoulder and said, “Maybe.” I thought that meant no, and I felt a bit silly for asking. Then I remembered that he does the one-shoulder thing when he's unsure or shy. So I asked, “Do you want to think about it, or is cricket not your thing?” He said, “I've never really played. I don't want to be bad.” I said I'd show him how to hold the bat at recess. He said, “Okay, maybe yes.” 🙂

qa.q: What did Chinmay say after lifting one shoulder?
qa.a: He said, “Maybe.”

qa.q: What did Thomas first think Chinmay's shoulder lift meant, and what did asking reveal?
qa.a: He first thought it meant no. Asking revealed that Chinmay was unsure and worried about being bad, since he had never really played.

qa.q: What small step helped clear up the maybe?
qa.a: Thomas asked a friendly, open question and offered to show him how to hold the bat, so Chinmay could say what was holding him back.

qa.q: How might Chinmay feel about being asked?
qa.a: Probably relieved that Thomas asked kindly and did not push, since he admitted his worry about being bad.

grounding: A one-shoulder lift is a weak signal of uncertainty or shyness; asking clarifies.

passage: At the village school, Nitin asked Hafsa if she wanted to fly kites with him on the roof after class for Sankranti. Hafsa lifted one shoulder and looked at her sandals. “Maybe.” Nitin wasn't sure. Was it a no, or a yes? Her cheeks looked pink, and she wasn't walking away. “Do you want me to bring an extra kite for you?” he asked. Hafsa glanced up. “I don't know how to launch it.” “I'll show you,” said Nitin. Her shoulder dropped, and she nodded.

qa.q: What holiday did Nitin ask Hafsa about the kites for?
qa.a: He asked her to fly kites for Sankranti.

qa.q: What might Hafsa's one-shoulder lift have meant, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Likely uncertainty or shyness about not knowing how to launch a kite, since she looked at her sandals and her cheeks were pink. It could also have been a half-hearted maybe that meant no.

qa.q: What did Nitin do that helped clear things up?
qa.a: He noticed she was not walking away, and he asked a friendly question that offered help, so she told him what worried her.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel when Nitin offers to show her?
qa.a: Probably relieved and a bit less shy, since her shoulder dropped and she nodded.

grounding: A one-shoulder lift is a weak signal of shyness or uncertainty; asking clarifies.

passage: At the village school parade, Charu stood in line with her hands behind her back, as Sir had taught, chin up. The flag went up, and the whole row stood the same way. Afterwards a peon told Charu that the headmaster wanted to see her. She stood outside his door, hands behind her back again, fingers tightly locked. Her friend Lavanya whispered, “Why are you hiding your hands? What did you do?” “Nothing!” said Charu, “I don't know why he called me.” The door opened. The headmaster was smiling. “Charu, your poem won the district prize.”

qa.q: What did the peon tell Charu after the parade?
qa.a: He told her that the headmaster wanted to see her.

qa.q: What might Charu's hands behind her back mean outside the door, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Probably nervousness, since her fingers were locked and she did not know why she was called. It could also be the parade habit of respect; it does not mean she had done something wrong.

qa.q: What would help Lavanya read the gesture better?
qa.a: Look at the context, the door and Charu's face, and ask kindly what is wrong instead of assuming guilt.

qa.q: How might Lavanya's question feel to Charu?
qa.a: It may have added to her worry, since she said she had done nothing. A gentler question would have felt more supportive.

grounding: Hands behind the back may signal respect, nervousness or concealment; it is not proof of guilt.

passage: On the school trip to the museum in Lagos, Emeka walked past the glass cases with his hands clasped behind his back. Wei, next to him, noticed and nudged him. “Why are your hands hidden? Did you take something?” Emeka rolled his eyes. “No. If I don't put them behind me, I'll touch things. Mum says I always do.” Wei laughed. The guide, who had overheard, smiled and said, “That's a good trick. The glass is there to protect the old pots.” Emeka kept his hands behind him and stared at the pots.

qa.q: Where was the school trip?
qa.a: The school trip was to the museum in Lagos.

qa.q: Why did Emeka keep his hands behind his back, and what did Wei first think?
qa.a: He was reminding himself not to touch things, since he says he always does. Wei first wondered if he had taken something, which shows how the gesture can be misread.

qa.q: What did Wei do that helped, and what could he do next time?
qa.a: He asked Emeka directly and laughed, which cleared it up. Next time he could ask more gently before suggesting anything about taking things.

qa.q: How might the guide see Emeka's clasped hands?
qa.a: As a sensible way to avoid touching the old pots, and as respect for the exhibits.

grounding: Hands behind the back can signal respect or self-control; it is not proof of guilt.

passage: Santosh's diary, Monday, after school. Hansa Ma'am was standing at the door this morning with her hands on her hips, and I thought, Uh-oh, she's angry that we're late. My stomach dropped and I stopped walking. But then she said, in her usual bright voice, “Good morning, quiz champions! Ready for the quiz?” She was catching her breath after climbing three floors with the papers. I had made up the whole angry thing. I think I'll listen to the words first next time, not only look at her hands. 😅

qa.q: How many floors had Hansa Ma'am climbed with the papers?
qa.a: She had climbed three floors.

qa.q: What did Santosh first think Hansa Ma'am's hands on her hips meant, and what did it turn out to be?
qa.a: Santosh first thought it meant she was angry that they were late. It turned out she was catching her breath after the stairs, and her bright words showed she was not angry.

qa.q: What can Santosh do next time?
qa.a: Listen to the words and tone as well as looking at her hands, as planned, and wait a moment before deciding she is upset.

qa.q: How might Hansa Ma'am feel if she knew the class had feared she was angry?
qa.a: Perhaps surprised and a little amused, since she was only resting after the climb. She might be glad to reassure them with her cheerful voice.

grounding: A teacher's hands on hips can look like authority or impatience but may be resting; tone and words add meaning.

passage: In the schoolyard of the village school, Saurabh Sir stood with his hands on his hips while the children ran back in from the well. Sonali slowed down. Sir is going to shout, she thought. Some children kept running. But Sir looked at the sky and said in a calm voice, “Clouds are coming. Line up, everyone, quickly, and we'll finish the lesson under the banyan.” His hands dropped as he waved them toward the tree. Sonali let out a breath. He had only been watching the sky.

qa.q: Where did Saurabh Sir tell the children to finish the lesson?
qa.a: He told them to finish the lesson under the banyan.

qa.q: What did Sonali first think Saurabh Sir's hands on his hips meant, and what did it turn out to be?
qa.a: She thought he was about to shout, and she slowed down. It turned out he was watching the sky and thinking about the weather.

qa.q: What could Sonali do next time she is unsure about a stance like that?
qa.a: Wait for his words and tone before deciding, and if she is unsure, ask calmly.

qa.q: How might Saurabh Sir see his own stance?
qa.a: As just standing and watching the sky, without realising it looked stern to some children.

grounding: A teacher's hands on hips can read as impatience but may mean nothing; tone and words give the meaning.

passage: On a cold morning in Cape Town, Thabo and Lucia sat outside the ice-cream stand. Thabo rubbed his hands together, fast, eyes on the seller. Lucia snapped her fingers in time to the radio. “Are you cold or excited?” she asked. “Both,” said Thabo. “Hot chocolate!” He snapped his fingers at the seller. “Hey!” The seller frowned. Lucia winced. “Try ‘Excuse me’,” she whispered. Thabo went red. “Excuse me, please, could I have two hot chocolates?” The seller smiled slightly. “Coming up.”

qa.q: What did Lucia snap her fingers in time to?
qa.a: She snapped her fingers in time to the radio.

qa.q: Why was Thabo rubbing his hands together, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: He said he was both cold and excited, and his eyes were on the seller, so it was likely a mix of cold and eagerness for hot chocolate. Rubbing hands can mean either alone.

qa.q: What could Thabo try next time to get a seller's attention?
qa.a: Say “Excuse me, please” and wait for eye contact, as he did on the second try, rather than snapping.

qa.q: How might the seller have felt when Thabo snapped his fingers?
qa.a: Probably annoyed or disrespected, since he frowned. The seller relaxed when Thabo asked politely.

grounding: Snapping fingers and rubbing hands have different meanings depending on context, and snapping at people can seem rude.

passage: In the sports hall before the kabaddi match, Divyansh rubbed his hands together, fast, and bounced on his toes. The hall was cold, and he was also dying to start. “Eager or freezing?” his teammate Mohit teased. “Both!” Mohit snapped his fingers at the coach across the hall to get his attention. The coach looked over slowly. “I'm not a waiter, Mohit.” Mohit's face went hot. “Sorry, Coach. Could you tell us where to stand?” “Better. Left side, both of you.” Divyansh grinned and rubbed his hands again.

qa.q: Where did the coach tell Divyansh and Mohit to stand?
qa.a: He told them to stand on the left side.

qa.q: Why was Divyansh rubbing his hands, and what else could explain it?
qa.a: He was probably eager to start, and the cold hall could explain it too. He says it is both.

qa.q: What could Mohit do instead of snapping his fingers?
qa.a: Say “Coach” or “Sorry to interrupt” and ask his question politely, as he did on the second try.

qa.q: How might the coach have felt when Mohit snapped his fingers at him?
qa.a: Probably a bit annoyed, since he said he was not a waiter. He was happy when Mohit asked politely.

grounding: Snapping fingers and rubbing hands mean different things by context; snapping at people can seem rude.
